summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, hygienic face shave with a changeable-blade straight razor: consult the client, check for conditions that stop or change the shave, prepare the skin with a hot towel and lather, shave with the correct holds and strokes, and finish and advise the client. You will also learn to handle single-use blades and the sharps container, deal with a nick, adapt the shave for razor bumps, and work safely with disinfectants and electrical equipment.

blocks.p: A face shave is one of the oldest services in barbering, and the one with the least room for error. You work with an open blade on a client's face and throat, and even a perfect shave removes a fine layer of skin cells along with the hair. A small slip draws blood, and blood can carry serious infections. That is why this unit is about **hygiene, blade safety and judgement** as much as razor skill.

The unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. It covers a full shave of the face and neck, a neck shave, and outlining the edge of a beard with the razor. Most of the clients you will shave have tightly curled beard hair, so you will also learn how to shave clients who get razor bumps, and when not to shave them at all.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks. In the first you set up a hygienic station, consult using contraindication cards, handle blades and the sharps container, and practise strokes by shaving a lathered balloon. In the second you give a full face shave to a model who has agreed in writing, under the assessor's close supervision.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Never shave a person at the Centre unless the assessor or instructor is watching. Photos of a shave show only the work area (jaw, cheek or neck), never the eyes or whole face, unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Shaving can break the skin without anyone noticing, so every face shave is treated as if blood were present. Blood and body fluids can carry viruses such as **hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV**. Skin and tools can also pass on bacteria (impetigo, infected follicles), fungi (barber's itch) and viruses (cold sores). Hygiene protects the client, the next client and you.

head: Word
What it does
In a face shave
rows: Cleaning

Washes away dirt, hair, lather and grease with soap or detergent and water. It does not kill all germs, but it must **always come first**, because germs hide under dirt and disinfectant cannot work through it.
The razor handle, bowl and brush are washed after each client.
Disinfecting
Kills **most** germs on a cleaned tool or surface, using an approved disinfectant for the **contact time on its label**.
The cleaned handle, bowl and brush are disinfected; the chair arms, headrest and trolley are wiped with disinfectant.
Sterilising
Kills **all** germs, including spores, usually with an autoclave (steam under pressure).
Used where the Centre has an autoclave and the maker says a tool can take it. The blade is never sterilised for reuse: it is thrown away.

blocks.note: Contact time is how long the tool must stay wet with, or covered by, the disinfectant. It is often several minutes, but it is whatever the label says. Dipping a tool in and out does nothing. Mix the disinfectant fresh, at the strength on the label, as often as the label says.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
Rule
rows: Razor blade
Single-use. One blade, one client, then straight into the sharps container.
Towels
Clean for each client. Used once, then into the laundry bin and washed hot.
Neck strip
The paper strip round the neck, under the gown. New for each client; thrown away.
Headrest cover
A fresh paper or towel cover on the headrest for each client.
Gloves
A new pair for each client. Nitrile gloves are widely used: they resist many chemicals and contain no latex, which some people are allergic to.
Tissues, cotton pads, spatulas
Single-use; thrown away.
Gown or cape
Clean, and kept off the skin of the neck by the neck strip.

ul: Wash your hands with soap and water before and after every client, then put on fresh gloves.
**Gloves protect both people** if the skin is cut and bleeds. Change them if they tear, and after dealing with blood.
Gloves, and an apron or eye protection where needed, are **PPE: personal protective equipment**.
Cover any cut on your own hands with a waterproof plaster under the glove.
Many barbers choose to be vaccinated against hepatitis B. Ask at a health centre or your doctor.

Take shaving cream from a **pump**, or from a tub with a **clean single-use spatula**. Never dip a used brush or your fingers into the tub: that carries one client's germs into the product for everyone after him.
Put what you need for one client into a clean bowl. Throw away what is left; do not put it back.

The **shaving brush** is washed in warm soapy water after each client, disinfected for the label's contact time, rinsed, shaken out and dried with the bristles down. A brush that stays wet grows germs. Some barbers apply lather with gloved hands instead.
Aftershave, oil and balm are poured or pumped onto your gloved hand or a pad, never applied from the bottle onto the skin.
Chair, arm rests, headrest and trolley cleaned and wiped with disinfectant before each client.
Tools laid out on a clean towel or tray, in the order of use.
A sealed blade, the **sharps container within reach**, a lined bin with a lid, and the laundry bin close by.
Styptic, cotton pads and spare gloves ready before you start, not fetched while a client bleeds.

head: Razor
What it is
Points to know
rows: Changeable-blade straight razor
A straight razor handle that holds a thin, single-use blade.
The one used at the Centre. **A new blade can be used for each client**, which cuts the risk of passing on infection. The handle is cleaned and disinfected between clients.
Fixed-blade straight razor (cut-throat)
The traditional razor: one solid blade, sharpened and stropped by the barber.
The same edge touches every client, and it is hard to make safe between them. Many shops and training centres no longer allow it for client work.
Trimmers and clippers
Electric tools.
Used to trim a long beard before the shave and to tidy outlines. Cleaned, disinfected and oiled between clients.

blocks.h: Loading, using and removing a blade

flow: Wash hands; put on gloves
Check the handle has been cleaned and disinfected
Show the client the sealed blade and open the wrapper in front of him
Hold the blade by its blunt parts only
Load it as the maker's instructions say and check it is seated and locked
Close the razor whenever it is not in your hand shaving
After the shave, open the holder over or beside the sharps container
Let the blade drop straight in, fingers clear of the edge
Clean, then disinfect, the handle

ul: **Why open it in front of the client?** So he can see for himself that a fresh blade is being used. A blade opened in the back room could be anyone's.
Some blades are snapped in half to fit the holder. Do this **inside the paper wrapper**, as the maker shows, so your fingers never touch the edge.
Never test a blade on your skin or nail.
Do not bend, snap or wipe a used blade with your fingers.
If a blade is dropped, nicked or drags, change it. It still goes into the sharps container, and the same client gets another new blade.
An open razor is either **in your hand, shaving, or closed**. Never put it down open on the chair, the trolley, the client's chest or a towel.
Never pass an open razor to another person. Close it and put it down for them to pick up.
Never walk about with an open razor, and never leave a razor where a child can reach it.
Do not try to catch a falling razor. Step back and let it fall.
Keep your attention on the client. No phone, no turning to talk to someone else, while the blade is on the skin.

blocks.p: 'Sharps' are items that can cut or pierce the skin: razor blades above all. A **sharps container** (sharps box) is a strong, puncture-proof, clearly labelled box with a lid and a small opening, made for used blades.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Every used blade goes straight in, by the person who used it.
A loose blade in a bin or a towel cuts the cleaner or the laundry worker.
Keep it within reach of the chair, on a stable surface, out of children's reach.
The less distance a used blade travels, the safer.
Never push blades down, shake it, or reach inside.
The contents are sharp and may carry blood.
Stop filling it at the **fill line** marked on the side (usually about three-quarters full). Then close and lock the lid.
An over-full box lets blades stick out of the opening.
A full, closed container is collected by an **approved waste service**, as the Centre's and local rules say.
It must never go out with the ordinary garbage, where it can injure the people who collect it.
Never empty it into another container or reuse it.
It is made to be used once.

blocks.note: If you cut yourself on a used blade: let the cut bleed gently, wash it well with soap and running water, cover it, tell your supervisor at once, record it in the accident book, and get medical advice the same day.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The consultation has two aims: to learn what the client wants, and to check that his skin is safe to shave. Do it before you gown him fully, in good light, with clean hands.

flow: Greet and seat the client; read his record
Ask what he wants
Ask about skin, allergies, medicines and health
Look at the skin of the face and neck
Feel the beard: length, coarseness and direction of growth
Decide: go ahead, go ahead with care, or do not shave
Explain your plan and the price
Record it

head: Ask
Why it matters
rows: What would you like: a full shave, a neck shave, or the beard outlined?
Sets the service and the price.
Have you had any skin problems or reactions after shaving before? Do you get razor bumps?
Tells you whether to shave with the grain only, not too close, or not at all.
Any allergies, for example to nuts, fragrance or latex?
Some pre-shave oils contain nut oils; many aftershaves are perfumed; some gloves are latex.
Are you taking any medicine, or do you have a medical condition I should know about?
Blood-thinning medicine makes a nick bleed more and for longer. Diabetes can slow healing. Some skin creams and tablets make the skin thin and tender.
How do you usually shave, and how often?
Shows how the skin is used to being treated.
Have you been in strong sun, or had any treatment on your face, in the last few days?
Sunburnt or freshly treated skin must not be shaved or heated.

ul: Look over the cheeks, upper lip, chin, jawline and neck for redness, bumps, sores, crusts, rashes, moles and scars.
Run your fingertips over the beard in several places to find the **direction of growth** (the grain). The hair feels smooth when you stroke with the grain and rough against it.

The grain is not the same everywhere. It usually runs downwards on the cheeks, but on the neck and under the jaw it may run sideways, upwards or in a swirl. Check each area, because your first pass must go **with the grain**.
Note where the hair is coarsest, usually the chin and upper lip.

blocks.p: A **contraindication** is a condition that means a service must not go ahead, or must be changed. For a face shave, sort what you find into two groups.

head: Do NOT shave: explain tactfully and suggest a doctor
What you may see
rows: Impetigo (a bacterial infection)
Weeping sores or blisters with honey-coloured crusts, often around the mouth and chin. Very contagious.
Barber's itch (tinea barbae; a fungal infection of the beard area)
Red, scaly, ring-like patches, sometimes with swollen lumps, pus spots and loose or broken hairs. Contagious.
Cold sores (a viral infection: herpes simplex)
A tingling patch, then small blisters or a crusted sore on or near the lip. Contagious.
Boils and infected follicles
Red, hot, painful lumps or pus spots around the hairs.
Infected razor bumps
Bumps that are red, swollen, painful or full of pus.
Open cuts, grazes, sores or stitches
Any broken skin in the area.
Eczema or dermatitis that is broken or weeping
Red, dry, itchy patches that have cracked, bled or begun to weep.
Sunburn or a fresh burn
Red, hot, tender skin.
A rash, swelling or lump you cannot explain
When in doubt, do not shave.

head: Go ahead WITH CARE
How you adapt
rows: Moles, skin tags and warts
Shave carefully **around** them. Never cut over a raised mole: it bleeds freely, and a mole that is injured or changing should be seen by a doctor.
Old, healed scars
Shave lightly over flat scars; stretch the skin so the blade does not catch the edge. Work around raised (keloid) scars.
Mild razor bumps, with no infection
Shave with the grain only, not too close, with the skin not over-stretched; or leave short stubble with a trimmer.
Blood-thinning medicine
Lightest strokes, a first time over only, extra care at the chin and neck. Have styptic and pads ready.
Diabetes
Take the same care: a nick may heal slowly. Be gentle with heat.
Dry or sensitive skin; eczema that is calm and unbroken
Warm, not hot, towel; fragrance-free products; first time over only; alcohol-free balm.
Mild acne
Shave lightly around spots; do not cut the heads off. If the spots are many and inflamed, do not shave.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not tell a client what disease he has. Say quietly, away from other clients, what you have seen and that you cannot shave over it today for his own safety, and suggest that he sees a doctor. Offer to book him when it has cleared. Then clean and disinfect everything he touched, and wash your hands.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae)** are common in men with tightly curled beard hair. When a curly hair is cut very short, its sharp tip curls back **into the skin**, or grows sideways under it. The skin reacts as it would to a splinter: red or dark, itchy, sometimes painful bumps, mostly on the neck and under the jaw. They are not an infection and not contagious, but they can become infected and can leave dark marks and scars.

Three things make them worse: shaving **against** the grain, shaving **too close**, and **over-stretching** the skin, which lets the cut hair spring back below the surface. Section 'Shaving the face and neck' shows how to adapt the shave.

sections.title: Preparing the client, the skin and the beard

flow: Put a fresh cover on the headrest
Seat the client and put a fresh neck strip round his neck
Fasten the gown over the strip
Tuck a fresh towel across his chest, into the neck strip
Recline the chair and adjust the headrest so his head and neck are supported
Check he is comfortable
Wash your hands and put on gloves

ul: A **reclined** client with a supported head keeps still, and the skin of his face and neck lies flat for the blade.
Lower the chair back smoothly and tell him before you do it.
Ask him to keep still, to raise a hand if he needs to cough, sneeze or speak, and not to talk while the razor is near his mouth. A sudden movement can cause a cut.
Set the chair height so you can work with a straight back.

blocks.p: A razor cannot mow through long hair: it drags, pulls and clogs. If the client has a long or full beard and wants a clean shave, **trim it short first** with clean, disinfected clippers or a trimmer, then brush away the clippings.
Wipe the face and neck with a gentle cleanser or a warm, damp towel to remove sweat, oil, dust and old products. Clean skin lets you see what you are shaving and lets the lather reach the hair.

A hot towel **softens the beard hair and warms the skin**, so the hair cuts more easily and the shave is more comfortable. A dry beard hair is tough; once it has taken up warm water it is much easier to cut.

flow: Take a towel from the steamer or hot cabinet with clean hands or tongs
Wring out the extra water over the basin
Unfold it to let the first steam escape
Test it on your own inner wrist
Tell the client it is coming
Wrap it under the chin and over the cheeks and upper lip
Leave the nose uncovered so he can breathe
Press it gently to the skin; leave it for a minute or two
Ask whether the heat is comfortable
Remove it and go straight on to the next step

ul: Test **every** towel on your inner wrist, where the skin is thin and sensitive. Gloved fingers are a poor guide to heat.
If the client says it is too hot, take it off at once. Never tell him to bear it.
A dripping towel scalds, because very hot water runs out of it onto the skin. Wring it out well.
Do not use a hot towel on sunburnt, inflamed or very sensitive skin. Use a warm one, or leave it out.

blocks.note: Before you use an electric towel steamer or hot cabinet, check that the plug and cable are undamaged and that your hands are dry. Fill and empty it only as the maker says, keep the cable out of the walkway, and switch it off at the end of the day. In Jamaica, check that the label matches the socket: 110 V, or 220 V for some equipment, at 50 Hz.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Pre-shave oil** is a light oil put on the beard before the lather. It helps the blade to glide and protects dry or sensitive skin. Use a few drops only, and only if the client has no allergy to its ingredients: read the label, because some contain nut oils.

ul: Use warm lather, taken out hygienically (see 'Hygiene and infection control').
Apply it with a clean brush or gloved fingertips in **small circular movements**. This lifts the hairs away from the skin and works the lather in around each one.
Cover the whole area to be shaved in an even layer: cheeks, upper lip, chin, jaw and neck. Keep it out of the nostrils and off the lips.
Lather softens the hair further, holds water against it and lets the blade slide.
**Lather must stay moist.** If it dries on part of the face before you reach it, apply fresh warm lather there before you shave. Shaving through dry lather drags and scrapes the skin.
On a hot day or under a fan, lather one side at a time.

head: Point
What you do
Why
rows: The free hand
With dry fingertips, stretch the skin gently just behind or beside the blade so it is firm and smooth.
A blade catches and cuts loose, wrinkled skin. Dry fingers do not slip on the lather: dry them on a towel as you go.
Blade angle
A low angle, about 30 degrees to the skin.
Too steep and the blade scrapes and cuts; too flat and it slides over the hair without cutting.
Stroke
Short, light, smooth strokes, moving the blade forward with a slight slicing action.
Long strokes lose control over curves. Pressing hard, sawing or going back and forth cuts the skin.
Direction
First time over **with the grain**, in the direction the hair grows.
It is the gentlest way to cut the hair and the least likely to cause cuts, soreness and ingrown hairs.
Order
Work in a set order round the face and neck, so no area is missed or shaved twice by mistake.
A routine keeps you calm and the shave even.
The blade
Wipe the lather off the blade onto a clean tissue, held in your free hand or laid on the towel on his chest.
A clogged blade does not cut cleanly. Never wipe it on your glove or the gown.

blocks.p: 'Freehand', 'backhand' and 'reverse freehand' are the names of **ways of holding the razor** for different strokes. Changing the hold lets you keep the correct angle, shave with the grain and see what you are doing on every part of the face, without twisting your wrist or leaning over the client. Your instructor will show you each one; practise them on a lathered balloon before you ever shave a person.

head: Hold
How it works
Typical use
rows: Freehand
The razor is held like a pen laid flat, the edge facing the way of the stroke; the stroke moves towards you.
The most common hold: downward strokes on the cheek and side of the face nearest you.
Backhand
The hand is turned over, palm up, with the edge facing away from you; the stroke moves away from you.
Areas where a freehand stroke would mean reaching across the face or bending the wrist back.
Reverse freehand
Held as for freehand but turned so the stroke travels upwards.
Places where the hair grows upwards, such as parts of the neck.

flow: Check the grain in the area again
Tell the client you are starting; remind him to keep still
Stretch the skin with dry fingertips
Start with the side of the face nearest you: sideburn, cheek, jaw
Shave the other side
Shave under the jaw and the neck, following the grain there
Leave the chin and upper lip until last, so the coarsest hair softens longest
Relather any area that has dried before you shave it
Wipe the blade often

blocks.p: Many textbooks divide the face and neck into numbered shaving areas, each with its own hold and direction. Use the chart and the order your instructor teaches; the principles above stay the same.

ul: **Under the nose.** Ask the client to pull his upper lip down over his teeth, or lift the tip of the nose gently with your free hand. Use very short strokes.
**Around the lips and the corners of the mouth.** The skin is thin and folds easily. Stretch it well. No talking.
**The chin.** A tight curve with coarse hair. Stretch the skin up from above or have him pull his lower lip in; take tiny strokes round the curve.
**The jawline.** The blade crosses an edge. Stretch the skin upwards so you shave on a flat surface.
**The neck and Adam's apple.** Ask him to swallow and hold, or draw the skin gently to one side so the lump moves away from under the blade.
**Moles, scars and bumps.** Shave around, as agreed in the consultation.

blocks.p: The **second time over** is a second pass, made after the first to get a closer finish. It is not automatic. Look at the skin first: if it is calm, with no redness, rash or nicks, and the client is not prone to bumps, relather (or apply warm water and a little lather) and shave again **across the grain**, with even lighter strokes. Going against the grain gives the closest result but is the hardest on the skin. Do it only where the skin is tough and calm, where the client wants it and your instructor agrees, and **never on sensitive or bump-prone skin**.

blocks.h: Adapting the shave for razor bumps

head: What you find
What you do
rows: Bumps that are infected, swollen or full of pus
Do not shave the area. Suggest he sees a doctor.
Mild bumps; a history of bumps after shaving
Soften the beard very well: hot (or warm) towel and plenty of lather
Shave **with the grain only**: first time over, no second pass
Stretch the skin only lightly
Do not go over the same spot again and again
Never pick out or dig at ingrown hairs with the blade
Bumps keep coming back whatever is done
Offer to leave a short stubble with a trimmer instead of a razor shave. For many men this is the only thing that stops the bumps.

ul: A **neck shave** tidies the hair below the jawline or at the nape after a haircut. The same rules apply: lather, a new blade, stretched skin, with the grain.
**Outlining** is shaping the edge of the beard, moustache or hairline with the razor to give a clean, sharp line. Jamaican barbers usually call it a **line-up** (or shape-up, or edge-up).
Follow the natural line of the beard. Agree the cheek line and neck line with the client before you cut, and check that both sides match.
Use the tip of the blade lightly, with the skin stretched. Clear lather or shaving gel lets you see the line.
A line taken a little too high cannot be put back, so take off less and check.

flow: Stop shaving; close the razor and put it down safely
Stay calm and tell the client what has happened
Check your gloves are on and not torn
Press a clean, single-use cotton pad or tissue firmly on the cut until the bleeding stops
Apply styptic powder or liquid with a fresh piece of cotton
Bag the blood-stained cotton, tissues and gloves
Clean and disinfect any surface with blood on it
Wash your hands and put on fresh gloves
Carry on carefully, avoiding the cut
Record it in the accident book and tell the supervisor

ul: **Pressure first.** Most nicks stop within a minute or two of steady pressure. Do not keep lifting the pad to look.

**Styptic** is a product, often containing alum, that closes a small cut and stops the bleeding. Use a powder or liquid applied with single-use cotton. Never use a shared styptic pencil: it touches one client's blood and then the next client's cut.
Do not put alcohol-based aftershave on a cut. It stings and irritates.
Blood-stained items go into a **sealed bag and are disposed of as clinical waste**, as the Centre's rules say. A towel with blood on it is bagged separately for a hot wash.
If the blade is changed, the old one goes into the sharps container.
If the cut is deep, or still bleeding after about ten minutes of firm pressure, get first-aid help and medical advice. Expect a nick to bleed longer in a client on blood-thinning medicine.
The accident book entry gives the date and time, the client, what happened, what was done and who was told.

flow: Wipe away the last of the lather with a warm, damp towel
Check the face and neck by sight and touch for missed hairs and nicks
Tidy any missed hairs with a little fresh lather
Place a cool towel on the face for a moment
Pat the skin dry
Apply a suitable aftershave product
Remove the towel and neck strip; brush away loose hairs
Raise the chair slowly
Show the client the result in the mirror

ul: The **warm towel** removes lather and loose hair gently. The **cool towel** soothes and refreshes the skin and calms redness.
Check with your fingertips as well as your eyes: you will feel a missed patch before you see it.
Raise the chair slowly. A client who has been lying back can feel light-headed if he sits up fast.

head: Product
What it does
Use it for
rows: Alcohol-free aftershave balm
Soothes, cools and moisturises.
The safest choice for most clients, and the right one for sensitive skin, bump-prone skin and small nicks.
Alcohol-based aftershave or splash
Tightens and feels fresh, but stings and dries the skin.
Only calm, unbroken, oily or normal skin, and only if the client likes it.
Light, fragrance-free moisturiser
Puts back moisture without perfume.
Dry or very sensitive skin; clients with fragrance allergies.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Keep your hands off the shaved area; do not scratch or rub it.
Freshly shaved skin has lost its top layer of cells and takes in germs easily.
Moisturise gently with a mild, alcohol-free product.
Shaving dries the skin.
Protect the skin from strong sun: shade, a hat or sunscreen.
Newly shaved skin burns and darkens more easily.
Avoid strongly scented products on the area for the rest of the day.
Perfume and alcohol sting and irritate.
If you get razor bumps: exfoliate gently with a soft cloth or mild scrub in the following days; do not pick or squeeze; do not shave again too soon.
Gentle exfoliation frees hairs before they grow in. Picking causes infection and dark marks.
See a doctor if a bump or nick becomes red, swollen, painful or filled with pus.
It may be infected.
At home: a clean, sharp blade, shave with the grain, do not share razors.
Blunt, dirty or shared razors cause cuts, bumps and infection.

blocks.note: Give the advice in a sentence or two as you show him the mirror, and hand him an aftercare leaflet if the Centre has one. Write on his record what you advised.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Gloves still on: remove the blade and drop it straight into the sharps container
Used towels and gown into the laundry bin
Neck strip, headrest cover, cotton and tissues into the bin; anything blood-stained into a sealed clinical waste bag
Wash the razor handle, bowl and brush with soap and water
Disinfect them for the label's contact time; rinse if the label says
Dry them and store them covered
Wipe the chair, headrest, arm rests and trolley with disinfectant
Sweep up any hair
Remove gloves, bin them, wash your hands
Check the sharps container is below its fill line
Refill supplies; lay out fresh towels and a new sealed blade

blocks.p: Used towels are washed hot with detergent and dried completely before reuse. Never carry a used razor to the sink with the blade still in it.
Disinfectants and cleaners are chemicals that can harm skin, eyes and lungs if they are misused.

ul: Read the **label** and the **safety data sheet (SDS)** before you use a product. The SDS is the maker's sheet that gives a chemical's hazards, first aid and safe storage. The Centre keeps one for each chemical.
Mix a disinfectant only to the strength on the label, with water, adding the chemical to the water. Too weak does not kill germs; too strong damages tools and skin.
**Never mix two chemicals together.** Some mixtures, such as bleach with other cleaners, give off poisonous gas.
Wear gloves, and eye protection if there is a risk of splashes. Work where there is fresh air.
Keep chemicals in their own labelled containers, lids closed, in a cool place away from heat, sunlight, food and clients. Never in a drink bottle.
If a chemical splashes in the eyes, rinse with plenty of clean running water and get medical help. Take the label or SDS with you.
If it spills on skin, wash it off with plenty of water. Wipe up spills on the floor at once.
Before use, check the plug, cable and casing of the towel steamer, clippers and trimmer for cracks, bare wire and loose pins.
Use electrical equipment only with **dry hands**, and keep water away from plugs, sockets and extension cords.
Keep cables out of walkways and away from the chair's base and footrest.
Do not overload a socket with several heating appliances.
Faulty equipment is unplugged, labelled 'Do not use' and reported. It is not used, and not repaired by a trainee.

head: On the client's record
Example
rows: Date, client, service
07/11/2026, Mr P. Edwards; full face shave
Consultation findings
Tightly curled beard; mild bumps under the jaw, none infected; no allergies; no medicines
What was done
Warm towel, lather, first time over with the grain only; no second pass
Products
Fragrance-free shaving cream; alcohol-free balm
Nicks or reactions
None
Advice
Gentle exfoliation from day 2; no picking; see a doctor if bumps become infected

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Keep them private and secure, as Jamaica's data protection law requires, and do not discuss one client's skin with another.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and how each is used in a face shave.
I can list the items that must be fresh for every client.
I can take shaving cream out hygienically and care for the shaving brush.
I can explain why a changeable-blade razor is used and why the blade is opened in front of the client.
I can load, use and remove a single-use blade safely.
I can state the rules for the sharps container, including the fill line and disposal.
I can carry out a consultation and find the direction of beard growth.
I can name conditions that stop a shave and conditions that need care, and refer a client tactfully.
I can explain what causes razor bumps and how to adapt the shave or offer stubble instead.
I can gown and recline a client with his head supported.
I can prepare and test a hot towel and apply it with the nose clear.
I can lather hygienically and keep the lather moist.
I can describe the free hand, the blade angle, the stroke and the direction of the first time over.
I can name the razor holds and the areas that need extra care.
I can say when a second time over is suitable.
I can deal with a nick, dispose of blood-stained items and record the injury.
I can finish a shave, choose an aftershave product and give aftercare advice.
I can clean up the station and work safely with chemicals and electrical equipment.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason with each step. For example: 'I test the hot towel on my inner wrist, so that the client's face is not burnt.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A razor handle that takes a new single-use blade for each client.
Used on one client only, then thrown away.
A strong, puncture-proof, labelled box with a lid for used blades.
The mark on a sharps container that shows when it must be closed and sent for disposal.
Removing dirt, hair and lather with soap and water.
Killing most germs on a cleaned tool or surface with a chemical.
How long a tool must stay in or wet with a disinfectant, as its label says.
Personal protective equipment, such as gloves.
Disposable gloves that resist many chemicals and contain no latex.
The paper or cotton strip put round the client's neck under the gown.
The fresh paper or towel put on the chair's headrest for each client.
A condition that means a service must not go ahead or must be changed.
A contagious bacterial skin infection with honey-coloured crusts.
A contagious fungal infection of the beard area.
A blister or sore on or near the lip, caused by a virus.
Red, dry, itchy patches of skin; not shaved over when broken or weeping.
Bumps caused by curly hairs growing back into the skin.
The direction in which the beard hair grows.
A heated, damp towel that softens the beard and warms the skin before shaving.
An oil put on the beard before the lather to help the blade glide.
The warm foam of shaving cream or soap that softens the hair and lets the blade slide.
The brush used to put lather on the beard.
Ways of holding the razor for different strokes.
The first pass of the shave, made with the grain.
A second pass for a closer finish, made only if the skin allows.
A powder or liquid that helps stop the bleeding from a small nick.
Waste with blood or body fluids on it, bagged and disposed of separately.
The book in which any cut or injury at work is recorded.
A soothing, usually alcohol-free product applied after shaving.
The maker's sheet giving a chemical's hazards, first aid and safe storage.
Shaping the edge of the beard or hairline with the razor to give a sharp line.

c1.title: A groom's shave in Port Maria
c1.text: Andre Whyte, 29, is getting married on Saturday and comes to a barber shop in Port Maria, St Mary, on Thursday for a full face shave. His beard hair is short and tightly curled. He tells trainee barber Ricardo that he often gets bumps under his jaw after shaving; today there are a few small, dark bumps there, none of them swollen or sore. He says, 'Take it right down, against the grain, twice. I want it smooth for the photos.'

c2.title: A retired teacher in Constant Spring
c2.text: Mr Lloyd Bennett, 68, a retired teacher, comes for a shave at a shop in Constant Spring, St Andrew. He says he takes a tablet every day 'to thin the blood' since a heart operation. Trainee Jermaine shaves with light strokes, but at the point of the chin the blade leaves a small nick, which bleeds steadily. Jermaine's box of styptic powder is in the store room, and there is a styptic pencil in the drawer that the shop used years ago.

c3.title: A practice station in May Pen
c3.text: At the Centre's barbering area in May Pen, Clarendon, trainee Romario is setting up for his practical. To save time he has already loaded a blade into the razor in the store room. The sharps container on his trolley is packed to the top, with a blade showing at the opening. He scoops shaving cream from the tub with the brush he used on his last model, and when his instructor calls him he puts the open razor down on the arm of the chair.

c4.title: A sore chin in Bog Walk
c4.text: Mr Trevor Hinds, 34, a taxi operator, sits down at a shop in Bog Walk, St Catherine, and asks for a clean shave before a family function. Trainee Oshane sees a cluster of weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts on the chin and at one corner of the mouth. Mr Hinds says they came up four days ago and are spreading. The shop is full, and the chair next to him is occupied.

c5.title: After the beach in Montego Bay
c5.text: Mr Paul Keller, a visitor staying in Montego Bay, St James, books a hot-towel shave at a hotel barber shop. He spent yesterday on the beach, and his cheeks, nose and neck are red, hot and tender. Trainee Dane takes a towel from the steamer; water is dripping from it. The steamer's cable has a split in its outer cover near the plug, and it runs across the floor behind the chair.

questions.q: How should Ricardo respond to Andre's request for a shave against the grain, twice?
o: Do as asked, since the client has the final say over his own face
Explain the risk of bumps and offer one pass with the grain
Shave against the grain once only, as a fair middle course
Refuse the shave altogether because he has bumps under the jaw
questions.why: Against-the-grain and repeated passes cut curly hairs below the surface, so they grow back into the skin. Mild bumps with no infection do not stop the shave; they change it: with the grain, once, and not too close.

questions.q: While shaving under Andre's jaw, how should Ricardo use his free hand?
o: Stretch the skin as tightly as he can, for the closest cut
Keep it off the face, so that nothing pulls on the bumps
Press the bumps flat with a fingertip as the blade passes
Stretch the skin only lightly, enough to keep it smooth
questions.why: The skin must be firm enough for the blade to glide, but over-stretching lets the cut hair spring back below the surface, which is how ingrown hairs start. On bump-prone skin, stretch lightly.

questions.q: The bumps come back after every shave Andre has. What could Ricardo suggest for the future?
o: Short stubble kept with a trimmer, instead of razor shaves
A razor shave every second day, so that the hairs stay short
Picking out each ingrown hair with tweezers after shaving
A strong alcohol aftershave to harden the skin of the neck
questions.why: For many men with tightly curled beards, leaving the hair just above the skin is the only reliable way to stop it growing back in. Shaving more often, picking and alcohol all make bumps worse.

questions.q: Which advice should Andre take home for the days before the wedding?
o: Shave again at home on Friday night to keep the finish smooth
Squeeze any new bump early, before it has time to show
Rub the area gently with a soft cloth; do not pick at bumps
Put cologne on the neck twice a day to keep it clean
questions.why: Gentle exfoliation in the days after a shave helps free hairs before they turn in. Shaving again too soon, squeezing and perfumed products irritate the skin and cause the very marks he wants to avoid.

questions.q: What should Jermaine do first about the bleeding nick?
o: Fetch the styptic powder from the store room, then come back
Wipe the blood away with the towel on Mr Bennett's chest
Finish the chin quickly so that all the lather can be removed
Press a clean single-use pad firmly on it and hold it there
questions.why: Steady pressure with a clean pad is the first action for any nick, and it matters even more for a client on blood-thinning medicine. The client is not left bleeding while supplies are fetched, which is why they are laid out before the shave.

questions.q: Why must Jermaine not use the styptic pencil from the drawer?
o: A pencil is too weak to work on a client who takes medicine
It has touched other clients' blood and can pass on infection
Styptic of any kind must not be used on the skin of the chin
A pencil works only if the skin has first been wiped with alcohol
questions.why: A styptic pencil is pressed directly onto a bleeding cut, so a shared one carries blood from client to client. Styptic powder or liquid is applied with fresh, single-use cotton instead.

questions.q: After ten minutes of firm pressure the nick is still bleeding. What should happen now?
o: Get first-aid help and medical advice, pressure kept on
Apply a hot towel to the chin to help the blood to clot faster
Send Mr Bennett home with a tissue held against his chin
Carry on with the shave and deal with the cut at the end
questions.why: A cut that will not stop is beyond a barber's first aid, and blood-thinning medicine makes this more likely. Heat increases bleeding, and a client must not be sent away or shaved further while still bleeding.

questions.q: Knowing about the tablets from the consultation, which plan for Mr Bennett's shave was the most sensible?
o: A first and second time over, but with a brand-new blade for each pass
No shave at all, since any client on medicine must be refused
A first time over only, light strokes, first-aid items laid out
A normal shave, with an alcohol aftershave to seal the skin after
questions.why: Blood-thinning medicine is a reason for extra care, not a reason to refuse: fewer passes, the lightest touch, and pads and styptic ready at the chair. A second pass doubles the chances of a nick.

questions.q: What should Romario do about the blade he loaded in the store room?
o: Use it, but tell the model that it came from a sealed packet
Wipe it with disinfectant in front of the model before he starts
Put it in a sharps container and open a new one at the chair
Leave it in the razor for his next model later in the session
questions.why: The client must be able to see a sealed blade opened for him; otherwise he cannot know it is fresh. A blade is never disinfected for use or saved, and any blade that is taken out goes into a sharps container.

questions.q: What is the right action for the sharps container on Romario's trolley?
o: Press the blades down with a spatula to make more room
Tip half of the blades into the lined bin under the trolley
Carry on, since one more blade will still fit at the opening
Stop using it, report it and start a new container
questions.why: A container is closed at its fill line and sent for approved disposal; this one is past that point and blades are exposed. Blades are never pushed down, handled or put in the ordinary bin.

questions.q: Why is scooping cream from the tub with the used brush a hygiene fault?
o: It carries germs from the last model into cream for others
The bristles soak up cream, so the tub is emptied much faster
Cream taken from a tub is always too cold to soften the beard hairs
A used brush makes thin lather that dries quickly on the face
questions.why: Whatever was on the last person's skin is now in the product and will be spread on everyone after him. Cream comes from a pump or a clean single-use spatula, into a bowl for one client.

questions.q: Romario puts the open razor on the arm of the chair. What is the rule he has broken?
o: A razor must be handed to the instructor whenever she calls
A razor not in use must be laid on a clean towel, blade up
A razor is closed whenever it is not in the hand, shaving
A razor must go back in the disinfectant jar between strokes
questions.why: An open blade left on a chair, trolley or client can be knocked, sat on or grabbed. The razor is either in your hand shaving, or closed and put down safely.

questions.q: What do the sores on Mr Hinds's chin most likely point to?
o: Razor bumps from shaving too closely last week
A contagious skin infection, so no shave today
Dry skin that needs pre-shave oil and a warm towel
A shaving-cream allergy that calls for another brand
questions.why: Weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts that are spreading are typical of a bacterial infection such as impetigo. A barber does not need to name it: any weeping, crusted, spreading sore in the area means the shave must not go ahead.

questions.q: How should Oshane tell Mr Hinds?
o: Say loudly, 'I can't shave you, you have impetigo', so others keep clear
Say nothing about the sores and tell him the shop is fully booked
Start the shave on the cheeks and stop when he reaches the chin
Quietly explain he cannot shave over the sores and suggest a doctor
questions.why: The client is told the truth, privately and kindly: what was seen, why shaving would be unsafe, and that a doctor can help. A barber does not diagnose, announce it to the shop, lie, or shave part of an infected face.

questions.q: Mr Hinds has left. He sat in the chair, leaned on the headrest and had a neck strip and towel on. What must Oshane do before the next client?
o: Change the neck strip and towel; the chair itself needs nothing
Spray air freshener around the chair and then wait five minutes
Bin the strip, bag the towel, disinfect the chair
Wipe the headrest with the used towel and turn the cover over
questions.why: The infection can be carried on anything he touched. Single-use items are thrown away, laundry goes for a hot wash, the chair, headrest and arm rests are cleaned and disinfected, and Oshane washes his hands.

questions.q: What should Dane decide about Mr Keller's shave?
o: Not to shave or heat the sunburnt skin; offer a later date
To shave as booked, but with a cooler towel than usual
To skip the towel and shave dry, so the skin is not heated
To shave the neck only, where the skin is a little less red
questions.why: Sunburnt skin is damaged, inflamed and tender. Heat and a blade would hurt and injure it further, so the shave waits until the skin has healed.

questions.q: For any client, why is a dripping towel from the steamer a danger?
o: It cools down too fast to soften the beard hair properly
It makes the lather too thin to hold the hairs up
It wets the neck strip, which then has to be changed
Hot water runs out of it onto the skin and scalds
questions.why: The water held in an unwrung towel is at the steamer's temperature and runs onto the face and neck. The towel is wrung out, opened to release steam and tested on the barber's own inner wrist every time.

questions.q: What should be done about the steamer?
o: Wrap the split in tape and move the cable under the chair
Keep using it today and report the cable at the end of the shift
Unplug it with dry hands, label it 'Do not use' and report it
Use it only for towels that are lifted out with metal tongs
questions.why: A damaged cable on equipment that holds water is a shock risk, and a cable across the floor is a trip hazard. Faulty equipment is taken out of use at once, labelled and reported; trainees do not repair it.

questions.q: Halfway through a shave on a breezy day, the lather on the client's left cheek has dried to a crust. What should the barber do before shaving that cheek?
o: Shave it as it is, with slightly firmer strokes
Put fresh warm lather on that cheek
Wet the crust with aftershave on a pad
Scrape the dry lather off with the blade first
questions.why: Lather works only while it is moist: it softens the hair and lets the blade slide. Shaving through dried lather, or pressing harder, drags the blade and scrapes the skin.

questions.q: A barber leaves the client's chin and upper lip until the end of the first time over. What is the reason?
o: The lather is thickest there and needs time to thin out
Those areas are the least sensitive parts of the face
The hair there is coarsest, so it gets longer to soften
Nicks there bleed least, so they matter less at the end
questions.why: Chin and upper-lip hair is usually the coarsest on the face. Shaving it last gives the heat and lather more time to soften it, so it cuts with less pull. These are in fact among the most sensitive areas, so they need the most care.
